title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Biology Third Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: In Third Term you finish the study of micro-organisms: how they grow, how they help and harm us, the diseases they cause and how we control them. You then explore the habitats where living things are found: the sea, estuaries, fresh water, marshes, forests, grasslands and deserts, and how plants and animals are adapted to each. The term ends with reproduction in single-celled organisms and some invertebrates.

Read each unit, study the diagrams, and draw them in your notebook. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Growth of Micro-organisms and Their Beneficial and Harmful Effects
summary: How bacteria multiply, the four phases of bacterial growth, the methods used to measure growth, and the many ways micro-organisms help and harm us.

p: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: one cell divides into two, the two become four, then eight, and so on. This is asexual reproduction. The time a cell needs to divide into two is called the generation time. It is different for different organisms and depends on the supply of nutrients, the temperature, the gases available (for example oxygen) and the pH.
If bacteria are put in a fresh nutrient medium and counted over time, the number of living cells follows a pattern with four phases.
1. Lag phase: the cells are getting used to the new medium and make enzymes. They grow in size but do not yet divide much, so numbers stay about the same.
2. Logarithmic (exponential) phase: the cells divide steadily at a constant rate. The number doubles every generation time and the curve rises steeply.
3. Stationary phase: food runs low and wastes build up, so new cells formed are balanced by cells that die. The number stays constant.
4. Decline (death) phase: more cells die than are formed because food is used up and poisonous wastes have collected. The number falls.

img.alt: A graph of number of living cells against time with four phases: a flat lag phase, a steep rise in the log phase, a level stationary phase and a falling decline phase

p: Turbidity method: as bacteria multiply, a clear liquid culture becomes cloudy (turbid). The cloudiness is measured with an instrument and tells us how many cells are present.

Serial dilution method: a sample is diluted step by step (for example 1 in 10 each time), a little of each dilution is spread on nutrient agar, and the colonies that grow are counted. The count is then multiplied by the dilution factor.
Squared transparent paper (cellophane) method: a squared transparent sheet is placed over the culture or colonies and the cells or colonies in a number of squares are counted to estimate the total.

Bacteria in the gut of herbivores help to digest cellulose. In humans, bacteria in the intestine make vitamin K and some B vitamins (including B12). Bacteria and fungi are used to make antibiotics such as penicillin. They are used to make amino acids and vinegar. Bacteria turn milk into yoghurt, cheese and other products with different tastes and flavours. They break down sewage into harmless inorganic substances. Microbial cultures make enzymes for industry. Yeast is a leavening agent that makes bread dough rise. Some algae fertilise the soil. Some micro-organisms are grown to make single-cell protein (SCP) as food. Decomposers recycle nutrients in the soil, and nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium help crops.
They cause decay and spoilage of food. They damage materials such as wood, paper, textiles, rubber and some metals. They cause many diseases in humans, animals and plants (see the next unit).

title: Control of Harmful Micro-organisms and Vectors
summary: Ways of controlling harmful micro-organisms (heat, cold, drugs, salting, drying and sanitation) and how to control mosquitoes and houseflies.

p: Harmful microbes can be controlled by removing them, stopping their growth or killing them with physical agents or chemicals. Common methods:

1. High and low temperature: boiling or heating food, pasteurisation of milk (heating to a controlled temperature to kill harmful microbes without spoiling the quality), sterilisation of medical instruments, and freezing food, which slows the microbes down to a minimum.
2. Covering food to stop vectors and airborne microbes from reaching it.
3. Antibiotics such as penicillin, ampicillin, amoxicillin and tetracycline are drugs that kill or stop the growth of many bacteria. They do not work on viruses.
4. Antiseptics such as Dettol, chlorine water, medicated soap and hydrogen peroxide kill microbes or stop them multiplying and are gentle enough to be used on skin.

5. Disinfectants are stronger than antiseptics and are used on floors, toilets and surfaces in hospitals, warehouses and public buildings. Examples are Izal and Lysol. Both antiseptics and disinfectants should be diluted as the label directs.
6. High salinity (salting): salt applied to meat and fish draws water out of the microbes by osmosis, so their cells shrink (plasmolysis) and die.
7. Dehydration (drying): microbes need water. Dried fish and meat do not support their growth.
8. Sanitation: keeping the body and the environment clean.
9. Isolation of infected persons, for example patients with tuberculosis or cholera, to stop the disease spreading.
10. A balanced diet every day helps the body to resist disease.
A bacteriostat stops the growth of bacteria; a bactericide kills bacteria. In the same way a fungistat stops fungi from growing and a fungicide kills them. A germicide kills germs in general.

sections.h: Vectors and how to control them
p: A vector is an animal that carries disease-causing organisms (pathogens) from one person to another.

Control of mosquitoes: drain swamps and stagnant water; clear bushes around houses; sleep under a mosquito net; spray rooms and swamps with insecticide; spray oil on water that cannot be drained (it blocks the breathing tubes of larvae and pupae); use insect repellent on the skin; take preventive drugs where advised; bury or cover broken pots and cans so they do not collect water.
Control of houseflies: spray with insecticide; destroy breeding places such as heaps of rubbish and dung; use poison baits; close or cover pit toilets; cover food; keep the environment clean.

title: Maintaining Good Health and the Roles of Health Organisations
summary: Refuse and sewage disposal, protecting water and food, and the work of the Ministry of Health, WHO, UNICEF, the Red Cross and UNESCO.

p: Refuse is the solid waste from homes and industries. Reckless dumping gives bad smells and gives breeding places to insects and rodents that spread diseases. Good ways to dispose of refuse: provide dustbins in good places; burn it in incinerators; dump it in an isolated area far from houses; bury it in a sanitary landfill. Recycling also reduces waste.

Sewage is waste water from kitchens, laundries, bathrooms and toilets, together with urine and faeces. It can be disposed of in pit latrines (deep pits for faeces and urine), in septic tanks (water flushes the waste into a large tank dug in the ground) or by a community treatment plant, where sewage from many homes is collected and treated before it is let into rivers or the sea.

Unclean water spreads cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea. Water can be protected and made safe by adding alum (which makes dirt settle), boiling before drinking, filtering after it cools, adding chlorine to kill germs, and storing it in clean covered containers.

Keep food in a refrigerator or deep freezer; cook food properly; inspect food sold to the public; wash hands before and after eating; preserve food by canning; keep the place where food is prepared clean; keep food away from flies and dust.

In Nigeria, health services are run through the Federal and State Ministries of Health and the University Teaching Hospitals. Countries also work together through international organisations to control disease and to give aid in the form of drugs, equipment and money.

title: Habitat: Meaning, Types and the Marine Habitat
summary: What a habitat is, the three main types, the three kinds of aquatic habitat, and the characteristics of the marine (sea) habitat.

p: A habitat is the place where an organism (plant, micro-organism or animal) is naturally found. For example, the habitat of a tadpole is the bottom of a freshwater pond or stream.
There are three main types. Aquatic habitat: in or around water. Terrestrial habitat: on or in the land. Arboreal habitat: on trees.

There are three kinds of aquatic habitat. Marine (salt water) habitat: oceans and seas. Brackish (estuarine) water habitat, where fresh water and salt water mix: deltas, lagoons and bays. Fresh water habitat, with little or no salt: lakes, rivers, streams and ponds.
1. It is the largest habitat in the biosphere, covering about 70% of the earth's surface.
2. It is the most stable habitat. Temperature, pH and density do not change suddenly.
3. It contains many dissolved ions, including sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺), chloride (Cl⁻), iodide (I⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻) and phosphate (PO₄³⁻).
4. Sea water is slightly alkaline. Its pH is about 8.0 near the surface. (The source notes say 8.0 to 9.0; the usual value is about 8.1.)
5. Salinity, the amount of dissolved salt, is high: about 35 parts per thousand.
6. Its density is higher than that of fresh water (about 1.028 compared with 1.0), so many organisms float easily.
7. The temperature of the sea changes more slowly than that of land, and it falls with depth.
8. Oxygen is highest at the surface where air dissolves in the water, and it decreases with depth.
9. Waves are movements of the surface water caused by wind. They mix the water and can wear away the shore.
10. Tides are the rise and fall of the sea surface at least twice a day, caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and the sun on the earth's water.

title: Zones of the Sea and Adaptations to Marine Life
summary: The horizontal and vertical zones of the sea, the organisms found in each, how plants and animals are adapted to marine life, and marine food chains.

p: The marine habitat consists of the shore and the open sea. From the shore outwards the zones are:
1. Splash (supratidal) zone: the area above the high-tide mark that is only wetted by splashes when waves break. It is exposed and often dry.
2. Intertidal zone: the shore between the high-tide and low-tide marks. It is covered by water at high tide and exposed at low tide. Temperature, salinity and moisture change greatly.
3. Subtidal (neritic) zone: always under water, over the continental shelf to about 200 m deep. There is plenty of sunlight and nutrients, so it holds the richest life in the sea.
4. Oceanic (open sea) zone: the deep water beyond the continental shelf.

On the sea floor, the benthic zone is the bottom. In the deep ocean (the abyssal zone, about 4000 to 6000 m) and in deep trenches (the hadal zone, below about 6000 m) there is no light and no photosynthesis. Producers are absent, so food is made mainly by chemosynthesis near vents and the animals depend on food that sinks from above.
Euphotic zone: the top layer, in direct sunlight (about 0 to 200 m). Producers, consumers and decomposers all live here and photosynthesis takes place.
Disphotic zone: the middle layer with dim light (about 200 to 1000 m). There is too little light for photosynthesis, so only consumers and decomposers live here.
Aphotic zone: the deep, cold, dark water and sea floor with no light and few living things.

img.alt: A cross-section of the sea from the shore with splash, intertidal and subtidal zones, then the oceanic zone, with euphotic, disphotic and aphotic layers by depth
img.cap: The zones of the marine habitat.

p: The source notes join several names in a confusing way (for example 'intertidal or neritic' and 'subtidal or littoral'). In standard biology the intertidal (littoral) zone is the shore between the tide marks, and the neritic zone is the shallow sea over the continental shelf. Learn the zones in the order shown in the diagram.

Splash zone: periwinkles, ghost crabs, seaweeds. Intertidal zone: starfish, sea anemones, sponges, sea urchins, annelid worms, molluscs and barnacles. Subtidal zone: snails, crabs, lobsters and crayfish. Neritic water: plankton (tiny floating organisms such as diatoms, algae, protozoa and small crustaceans) and nekton (strong swimmers such as fish, prawns and whales). Oceanic water: sharks, croaker, mackerel, bonga fish and many more. Benthic zone: only a few scavengers and saprophytes.
Barnacles have a protective shell that stops drying out (desiccation) and holds water, and they attach firmly to rocks. They feed with their cirri (feathery limbs).

Fishes: cartilaginous fish such as sharks keep urea in their blood so that their body fluids are as salty as the sea; bony fish such as tilapia have salt-secreting cells in the gills to keep their salt balance (osmoregulation). Fins give movement and balance; gills are for breathing.
Starfish have tube feet for holding on to rocks and moving.

Whales have fins for stability, a thick layer of fat (blubber) for insulation and food storage, and blowholes for breathing air. (The source notes say whales have 'an organ in front of the nostril' for sensing pressure.)

Shrimps have strong claws for holding food. Periwinkles have a foot for attaching to rocks and a shell. (The notes say periwinkles have lungs; marine periwinkles breathe with gills.) Crabs burrow into mud to hide from predators and strong waves.

Seaweeds have a holdfast for attaching to rocks, a slimy (mucilaginous) coating that prevents drying, and air bladders or divided fronds for floating. Algae such as Sargassum have chlorophyll for photosynthesis and small size or large surface area for floating. Plankton such as diatoms are tiny and have air spaces or oil droplets to keep them afloat.
Diatom → crab → tilapia. Diatom → zooplankton → tilapia → shark.

title: The Estuarine (Brackish Water) Habitat
summary: What an estuary is, its characteristics, its plants and animals and how they are adapted, and food chains in estuaries.

p: An estuary is a body of water formed at the coast where fresh water flowing towards the sea mixes with sea water coming inland. It is a brackish water habitat. Examples are deltas, lagoons and bays, such as the Lagos Lagoon and the Niger Delta.
1. The salinity changes with the tides and with the season (it falls in the rainy season and rises in the dry season).
2. The density of the water is less than that of sea water.
3. The water is turbid (muddy) because it is often disturbed, so light penetration, photosynthesis and respiration by organisms are reduced.
4. The water is shallow.
5. There are fewer kinds of species than in the sea.
6. It has a high level of nutrients carried down by rivers.
7. Oxygen in the mud is low, so anaerobic activities are common.
Plants found in estuaries include plankton (diatoms), algae, red mangrove and white mangrove.
Plankton such as diatoms have air spaces in their cells for buoyancy. Algae have chlorophyll for photosynthesis and a small size or large surface area for floating.

Red mangrove has stilt roots that support the plant in soft mud and stop the tide from washing it away. Its roots have air spaces that carry air to the root tissues. Its seeds germinate while still on the parent plant (this is called vivipary), so the young seedlings drop into the mud and are not carried away by the water.
White mangrove has pneumatophores (breathing roots) that stick up out of the mud for gaseous exchange.

Mosquito larvae and pupae have breathing tubes (siphons or 'trumpets') that reach up to the surface. Crustaceans and water snails burrow into the mud to hide from predators, strong waves and tides. Worms have a tough, waterproof covering against changes in salinity. Mudskippers have strong fins for crawling on mud and swimming in water, and can breathe air through their skin. Fishes have fins for swimming and a swim bladder for buoyancy.
Detritus (dead organic matter) → worms → snails → birds. Diatoms → shrimps → fishes. Diatoms → small fish → sharks → man.
